overview: Both are biological regulators, but enzymes speed up chemical reactions while hormones send signals between cells.
genZNote: Enzyme is the reaction's personal trainer, speeding things up. Hormone is the messenger texting instructions to distant cells.

aspects.label: Chemical Nature
aspects.valueA: Almost always a protein (a biological catalyst).
aspects.valueB: Can be a protein, peptide, steroid, or amino-acid derivative.

aspects.label: Function
aspects.valueA: Catalyses (speeds up) a specific biochemical reaction without being consumed.
aspects.valueB: Acts as a chemical messenger, regulating the activity of target cells/organs.

aspects.label: Site of Action
aspects.valueA: Acts at or very near its site of production (often intracellularly).
aspects.valueB: Produced in one location (a gland) but often acts at a distant target organ.

aspects.label: Consumed in the Reaction?
aspects.valueA: No — an enzyme is reused repeatedly.
aspects.valueB: Hormones are used up/degraded after signalling and must be continuously produced.

overlay.examHighYieldNote: An enzyme lowers activation energy without being consumed, while a hormone is consumed/degraded as part of its signalling role.
overlay.memoryTrick: Enzyme = catalyst, speeds reactions. Hormone = messenger, sends signals.
overlay.commonMisconception: Not all hormones are proteins — steroid hormones like cortisol and oestrogen are lipid-based, not protein-based.
